title: One cell, many jobs: how a baby's body gets built

summary.text: Nearly every cell in your body holds the same full set of instructions. So why is one cell part of a fingernail and another part of your eye? In the womb, cells find their job from their place among their neighbours. A signal spreads from one spot and gets weaker with distance, and each cell reads how much has reached them. Your child tests this idea with strips of paper and dye. They also find out why the gaps between fingers are made by cells that die, how a baby breathes without air, why growth is fast and then slows, and how practice rewires a brain.
summary.art: A flat paper strip dipped at one end in red dye, dark at the dipped end and fading to pale at the far end, with a tiny embryo hand drawn above it.

intro.hook: Spread your fingers wide and look at the gaps between them. Before you were born, there were no gaps. Your hand was a flat paddle, like a tiny oar. What made the gaps?
intro.text: Nothing was cut and nothing was glued. Cells between the fingers received a signal, and they died on purpose. That left five fingers. In this unit you find out how a body is built from one cell. You test how cells can learn where they are, from a signal that fades with distance. You time yourself writing with the wrong hand, to see how practice changes a brain. You also learn how a baby breathes and eats before birth, and why growth is fastest at the very start.
intro.art: A child's open hand beside a drawing of a tiny embryo hand shaped like a flat paddle with faint finger lines.

outcomes: I can explain that every cell in a body holds the same instructions, but each kind of cell uses different parts of them.
I can describe how a signal that fades with distance lets cells find out where they are, and so what job to take.
I can use a model, say what it shows and what it does not show, and write my claim, my evidence and my reasoning.
I can explain how a baby gets oxygen and food through the placenta, and what changes at the first breath.
I can explain that cells die on purpose while a body is built, for example between the fingers.
I can read a line graph of growth and say when a baby grows fastest and how growth slows.
I can explain how practice changes the connections in a brain, and why a young child has more connections than an adult.
I can describe how Hilde Mangold's experiment showed that neighbours tell cells what to become.

terms.meaning: A very long molecule inside nearly every cell. It holds the instructions for building and running a body.
terms.example: If you stretched out the DNA from one of your cells, it would be about two metres long.
terms.art: A twisted ladder shape coming out of a tiny cell, with a two-metre ruler beside it.

terms.meaning: One instruction on the DNA. Most genes tell a cell how to make one kind of protein, which is a building block or a worker in the body.
terms.example: One gene tells red blood cells how to make haemoglobin, which carries oxygen.
terms.art: A long thread of DNA with one short stretch glowing and an arrow to a small protein shape.

terms.meaning: A cell that can divide to make more cells and that has not yet settled on a final job. Some stem cells can become many kinds of cell.
terms.example: Stem cells in your bone marrow make new blood cells every day.
terms.art: One round cell in the middle with arrows to a blood cell, a skin cell and a nerve cell.

terms.meaning: A cell that has settled on one job and has a shape that suits that job. People have more than 200 kinds.
terms.example: A nerve cell is long and thin to carry signals. A red blood cell is a round disc to carry oxygen.
terms.art: Four cells side by side: a long nerve cell, a round red blood cell, a flat skin cell and a muscle fibre.

terms.meaning: A chemical message that one cell sends and other cells can sense. Cells use signals to tell neighbours what to do.
terms.example: A signal released in a growing embryo can tell nearby cells to become bone.
terms.art: A cell sending out small dots to the cells around it, which turn to face the dots.

terms.meaning: A change that goes smoothly from a lot to a little over a distance. The amount of a signal falling away from its source is a gradient.
terms.example: The smell of tadka is strong in the kitchen and weaker in the next room.
terms.art: A row of squares coloured from deep red at the left to pale pink at the right.

terms.meaning: A baby in the first eight weeks of growing, while the main parts of the body are being laid down.
terms.example: At week four, an embryo is a small curved shape with a beating heart.
terms.art: A tiny curled embryo with a small heart bump and arm buds, drawn beside a grain of rice for size.

terms.meaning: A baby from the ninth week of growing until birth. By then every main part has begun, and the baby mostly grows bigger.
terms.example: A foetus kicks, swallows and hears long before birth.
terms.art: A curled foetus floating in the womb with the cord running to the placenta.

terms.meaning: Cells dying on purpose, when a signal tells them to, as part of building or caring for a body. The scientific name is apoptosis.
terms.example: The cells between your fingers died before you were born, and that left five separate fingers.
terms.art: A paddle-shaped hand with grey cells between the finger lines fading away.

terms.meaning: A small group of cells in an embryo that sends signals telling nearby cells what to become. Hilde Mangold found the first one, in work published in 1924.
terms.example: A piece of organiser tissue moved to the wrong place made a second body start to grow there.
terms.art: A tiny newt embryo with a small patch marked on its back and an arrow to a second body axis.

terms.meaning: A flat, soft organ that grows in the womb during pregnancy. It passes oxygen and food from the mother's blood to the baby, and waste back.
terms.example: The placenta is about the size of a dinner plate at birth.
terms.art: A placenta like a round dish with branching fingers and the cord leading to a baby.

terms.meaning: A red protein inside red blood cells. It holds oxygen in the lungs and lets it go in the body.
terms.example: A baby before birth makes a kind of haemoglobin that holds oxygen more tightly than adult haemoglobin does.
terms.art: A red blood cell with small red molecules inside, each holding two oxygen dots.

terms.meaning: A firm but bendy material that is not as hard as bone. Many of a baby's bones begin as cartilage and slowly harden.
terms.example: You can feel cartilage at the tip of your nose and in your ear.
terms.art: A child bending the soft top of their ear, with a bone drawn beside it for comparison.

terms.meaning: A layer of growing cartilage near each end of a long bone. It makes the bone longer, and turns to bone when growing stops.
terms.example: Your thigh bone gets longer at its growth plates, until you are in your late teens.
terms.art: A long bone with a coloured band near each end labelled as the place where it grows.

terms.meaning: A soft spot in a baby's skull where the bones have not yet joined. It lets the head squeeze through birth and lets the brain grow.
terms.example: The big soft spot on top of a baby's head usually closes before the baby is two.
terms.art: A baby's head from above showing the soft diamond-shaped spot between the skull plates.

terms.meaning: The tiny gap where one nerve cell passes a signal to the next. A brain has a huge number of them.
terms.example: Each time you practise a skill, the synapses you use get stronger.
terms.art: Two nerve cells nearly touching, with tiny dots crossing the small gap between them.

terms.meaning: Two babies who began as one ball of cells that split in two early on. They have the same genes.
terms.example: Identical twins look alike, but they have different fingerprints.
terms.art: A ball of cells splitting into two balls, and two small babies growing from them.

explanations.concept: The same instructions in every cell
explanations.definition: Nearly every cell in your body holds a full copy of your DNA, and each kind of cell reads only some of the genes.
explanations.description: You began as one cell. That cell split in two, and each new cell got a full copy of the DNA. They split again, and again, and copied the DNA each time. Today you have about 30 trillion cells, and almost all hold the same set of about 20,000 genes. A gene is one instruction, usually for making one kind of protein. A skin cell uses the genes for skin proteins. A red blood cell uses the genes for haemoglobin. The other genes stay switched off, like pages in a cookbook that a cook does not open today. One surprising proof comes from frogs. In 1962 John Gurdon took the nucleus, which holds the DNA, from a cell in a tadpole's gut. He put it into a frog's egg cell whose own nucleus he had removed. A few of these eggs grew into healthy tadpoles, and later work made frogs. So the gut cell still held every instruction.
examples: A hair cell and a bone cell in the same person hold the same genes but use different ones.
A cloned animal such as Dolly the sheep (1996) grew from DNA taken from a cell in an adult's udder.
Red blood cells lose their DNA when they mature, so they are one of the few cells without it.
explanations.art: A cookbook with many pages, with a skin cell holding it open at the skin pages and a red blood cell holding it open at the haemoglobin page.

explanations.definition: Specialising is when a cell settles on one job, and uses only the genes for that job from then on.
explanations.description: In the first days, the cells in the growing ball are not yet different from each other. As the ball gets bigger, cells begin to choose different jobs. Scientists count more than 200 kinds of cell in a person. Each kind has its own shape that fits its work. Nerve cells are long and thin and carry signals. Muscle cells are long and can shorten. Red blood cells are small discs that carry oxygen. Some cells never fully settle. Stem cells stay ready to make new cells, for as long as you live. The stem cells in your bone marrow make about two million new red blood cells every second.
examples: Early cells in the ball can become any part of the body, and later cells can become only some parts.
Stem cells in the lining of your gut replace it every few days.
Skin cells are replaced as the top layer wears off.
explanations.art: A tree-like diagram with one cell at the top branching into many differently shaped cells at the bottom.

explanations.concept: A signal that fades with distance tells cells where they are
explanations.definition: In a growing embryo, some cells send out a chemical signal that spreads and gets weaker with distance, and nearby cells take different jobs depending on how much of it reaches them.
explanations.description: A body needs the right cells in the right places. A cell cannot see or measure. But a cell can sense a chemical. In 1969 the British scientist Lewis Wolpert had an idea. Suppose a small group of cells sends out a signal. Cells close by get a lot of it, cells farther away get less, and cells far away get almost none. Cells could read the amount, and each would know their distance from the source. Many scientists have since found signals that work in this way. In 1988 Christiane Nüsslein-Volhard and her team found one in a fruit fly egg, which tells the front of the baby fly from the back. Signals like this have been found in mice, chicks, fish and people. In humans, a signal called Sonic hedgehog helps to set the order of the nerve cells in the spine. Most of the detailed work was done on flies, frogs, chicks and mice, because their embryos are easy to study.
examples: A paper strip dipped in dye at one end is dark near the dye and pale far from it, so the colour tells you the distance.
In the spinal cord, cells close to the signal become one type of nerve cell and cells far away become another.
Your five fingers get their different shapes partly from how much of a signal reaches each one.
explanations.art: A row of cells beside a bright signal source at the left, with the cells shaded darkest near the source and palest at the far end, and three different cell jobs marked.

explanations.concept: Early cells can change their minds: identical twins
explanations.definition: Early in a baby's growth, cells have not yet settled on their jobs, so a ball of cells can split and each half can make a whole baby.
explanations.description: In 1891 the German scientist Hans Driesch shook apart the two cells of a sea urchin egg that had just divided. Each cell grew into a whole tiny sea urchin. Cells from the early ball are not fixed on being a left half or a right half. They follow what the cells around them are doing. Identical twins are the same idea in people. Very early on, the ball of cells splits in two, and each half builds a whole baby. Twins from one ball have the same genes. Non-identical twins come from two separate egg cells. They are as alike as any brother and sister. Later, cells do settle on their jobs. Cells from an older embryo that are moved keep the job they had, and do not take on the job of their new neighbours.
examples: Identical twins have the same genes, but different fingerprints and different personalities.
Non-identical twins can be a boy and a girl, because they came from two different cells.
Moved cells from an early embryo follow their new neighbours, and moved cells from a later embryo keep their old job.
explanations.art: A ball of cells splitting into two halves, and each half growing into a baby, drawn as two small curled babies side by side.

explanations.concept: Building by taking away: cells that die on purpose
explanations.definition: Programmed cell death is when cells receive a signal and take themselves apart, safely, as part of building a body.
explanations.description: Building a body is not only adding. Sometimes it is carving. Your hand began as a flat paddle. Around week six after you began, signals told the cells between the finger lines to die. By week eight your fingers were separate. The cells did not burst. They folded themselves up and were cleared away by neighbouring cells. A chick has separate toes, and the cells between the toes die. A duck has webbed feet, and in a duck most of those cells stay alive. A tadpole's tail also goes by cell death when the tadpole grows into a frog. Cell death does not stop after birth. Every day, your body removes tens of billions of old or worn cells, and stem cells make new ones to replace them. In 1972 John Kerr, Andrew Wyllie and Alastair Currie gave it the name apoptosis. In a few babies, some cells between fingers do not die. Then two fingers stay joined, and a small operation can separate them.
examples: Cells between your fingers and toes died before you were born.
A tadpole's tail disappears as the frog grows.
Every day your body clears away tens of billions of worn cells.
explanations.art: Three stages of a hand: a flat paddle, a paddle with grey cells between faint finger lines, and five separate fingers.

explanations.concept: The placenta: where two bloodstreams meet
explanations.definition: The placenta is an organ that grows in the womb. Blood from the mother and blood from the baby flow close together inside it, separated by a very thin wall.
explanations.description: A baby floating in water cannot breathe air or eat. The placenta does both jobs for them. The mother's blood flows through small pools inside the placenta. Inside the pools stand thousands of finger-like branches, which are full of the baby's blood. The cord carries blood between the baby and the placenta. The wall between the two bloodstreams is thinner than a hair, so oxygen and food pass through, and waste carbon dioxide passes back. Mother's blood and baby's blood do not mix. A baby can have a different blood group from their mother. The branches give the placenta a huge surface. Measurements differ, but one often-quoted estimate is about 12 square metres, about the floor of a small room, which is why exchange is fast. The baby's own cells build the placenta, from the outer layer of the early ball of cells. The placenta also makes hormones and passes antibodies from the mother. Some harmful things can cross too, such as alcohol and some germs. That is why doctors advise pregnant women about medicines and what to avoid.
examples: Oxygen flows from the mother's blood to the baby's blood, because the baby's blood holds oxygen more tightly.
Sugar and other food molecules cross the thin wall into the baby's blood.
After the baby is born, the placenta comes out of the womb a little later.
explanations.art: A cut-through placenta showing branching fingers full of red baby-blood inside pools of mother's blood, with arrows for oxygen going in and carbon dioxide going out.

explanations.concept: The first breath: how the body switches over
explanations.definition: At birth, the lungs fill with air for the first time, blood begins to flow through them, and the small shortcuts in the baby's heart and blood vessels close.
explanations.description: Before birth, a baby's lungs are filled with fluid and do not breathe air. Most of the baby's blood skips the lungs. It crosses through two small shortcuts in the heart and a nearby vessel. At birth, the squeezing of the journey helps push fluid out of the lungs. The baby cries, and breathes in. Air opens the lungs, and blood starts to pour through them. The pressure changes shut the shortcuts within days. The cord is no longer needed. Over the first six months, the baby also swaps the haemoglobin they made before birth for adult haemoglobin. The belly button is where the cord was.
examples: A baby's first cry is also the first time their lungs fill with air.
A premature baby may need extra oxygen, because the lungs are not yet ready for air.
The belly button is the small scar left by the cord.
explanations.art: Two heart drawings side by side: one before birth with a shortcut open, and one after birth with the shortcut closed and blood flowing through the lungs.

explanations.concept: Growth is not steady: fast, then slower, then a spurt
explanations.definition: A child grows quickly in the first two years, more slowly through middle childhood, and then quickly again in a growth spurt in the early teens.
explanations.description: A healthy baby grows about 25 centimetres in their first year, from about 50 to about 75 centimetres. In the second year they grow about 12 centimetres more. From age three until the teens, a child grows around five to six centimetres a year. Then comes a spurt, when the body can grow eight to ten centimetres in one year. Girls usually have the spurt earlier than boys. Long bones grow longer at their growth plates, the layers of cartilage near each end. Cartilage cells multiply and the new cartilage turns to bone. When growing ends, in the late teens, the growth plates close. In 2006 the World Health Organization published growth charts made from well-fed, well-cared-for children in six countries, Brazil, Ghana, India, Norway, Oman and the United States. The children grew in almost the same way. That shows that growth depends much more on food, care and health than on where a child lives.
examples: A baby's length grows about 11 centimetres in the first three months and about 4 centimetres in the three months after the ninth month.
A child of seven grows slowly but steadily, a few centimetres a year.
Many teenagers grow faster than at any time since they were babies.
explanations.art: A line graph of height against age that rises steeply at the start, flattens through childhood, bends up again in the teens, and then levels off.

explanations.definition: A newborn has about 300 bone pieces, many of them still partly cartilage. Over the years, pieces join and cartilage hardens until an adult has 206 bones.
explanations.description: A baby's skull is made of several plates that are not yet joined. The gaps between them are the fontanelles, or soft spots. During birth the plates can slide over each other, so the head can squeeze through the narrow passage. After birth the soft spots leave room for the fast-growing brain. The big one on top closes between about one and two years of age. The wrist begins as a handful of cartilage pieces that slowly harden into eight small bones. Doctors can read a child's age from an X-ray of the wrist, because the bones appear one by one. Many bones also join as you grow. The base of the spine, for example, begins as several pieces that fuse into one.
examples: A newborn's wrist is mostly cartilage, and an adult's wrist has eight hard bones.
The soft spot on top of a baby's head is covered by tough skin that protects the brain underneath.
A baby has about 300 bone pieces, and an adult has 206 bones.
explanations.art: A baby's skull from the side with soft spots shaded, next to an adult skull with the plates joined by wavy lines.

explanations.concept: The brain: born with more connections than we keep
explanations.definition: A young child's brain makes many more connections between nerve cells than it keeps. Connections that are used get stronger, and connections that are not used fade.
explanations.description: A newborn already has most of the roughly 86 billion nerve cells they will ever have. The brain weighs about a quarter to a third of an adult brain. By age three it is about four-fifths of the adult size, and by age five about nine-tenths. In those years, the number of synapses shoots up. In 1979 the neurologist Peter Huttenlocher counted synapses in brains and found that a young child has far more than an adult. Then the brain prunes. Synapses that are used often are made stronger. Synapses that are not used are removed. This is how practice works. When you practise a skill, you make particular connections stronger, and the skill gets faster and easier. London taxi drivers, who must learn the whole city, were found in 2000 to have a larger back part of the hippocampus, a part used for finding the way, than other adults. A brain is shaped by what it does.
examples: A baby who hears two languages keeps the sounds of both.
A skill such as riding a cycle feels hard at first, and then your connections strengthen and it feels easy.
Learning to write with the wrong hand gets quicker with each try.
explanations.art: Two nerve cell networks side by side: a dense tangle labelled as a young child, and a smaller network with a few thick, strong connections labelled as after practice.

explanations.concept: What shapes a person: genes, surroundings, or both?
explanations.description: Genes give the instructions, but a baby's surroundings change how the instructions are used. Scientists agree on this. They argue about how much each counts, and about how. In the winter of 1944 to 1945 the Netherlands had a famine called the Hunger Winter. Babies whose mothers were hungry in early pregnancy grew up with more health problems as adults, even though their genes were the same as their brothers' and sisters'. Scientists still debate exactly how the hunger left its mark.
examples: Identical twins have the same genes but are not the same.
A well-fed, well-cared-for child grows taller than the same child would with too little food.
A child's language comes from the people around them, not from their genes.
explanations.art: A small plant in two different soils, one tall and green, one short and pale, with the same seed packet beside both.

perspectives.explanation: Studies of twins find that height and many other features are very similar in identical twins, even when they are raised apart. The genes set the main plan.
Food, health, care and learning change how a body grows. The Hunger Winter showed that what a mother eats can shape a baby's health for life.

perspectives.who: Both together, in ways still being worked out
perspectives.explanation: Chemical tags on the DNA, which switch genes on and off, may carry the marks of early life. Scientists disagree on how large these marks are, and how long they last.

agreed.text: Nearly every cell in a body holds the full set of instructions, and each kind of cell uses only some of them.
agreed.evidence: In 1962 John Gurdon put the nucleus from a tadpole's gut cell into an egg cell, and a few of these eggs grew into healthy tadpoles and frogs. In 1996 Dolly the sheep was cloned from a cell in an adult sheep's udder.

agreed.text: Cells in an embryo find their jobs from signals sent by their neighbours.
agreed.evidence: In work published in 1924, Hilde Mangold and Hans Spemann moved a small piece of newt embryo and the neighbouring cells began to build a second body. Since then, signals have been found in many animals.

agreed.text: Cells die on purpose during growth, and this shapes the body.
agreed.evidence: In chicks, cells between the toes die and the toes are separate. In ducks, most of those cells live and the feet stay webbed.

agreed.text: The mother's blood and the baby's blood run close together in the placenta but do not mix.
agreed.evidence: A baby can have a different blood group from their mother. This could not happen if the blood simply mixed.

agreed.text: Healthy children grow in much the same way wherever they live, if they are fed and cared for.
agreed.evidence: The World Health Organization measured about 8,000 children in Brazil, Ghana, India, Norway, Oman and the United States, and published the growth standards in 2006.

agreed.text: Practice makes some connections in the brain stronger and unused ones fade.
agreed.evidence: Studies of the brains of young children and other young animals show that connections are most numerous early in life and are then pruned by use.

challenging.claim: Cells are born knowing what job they will do.
challenging.for: Roux killed one of two frog cells with a hot needle. The other cell grew into only half an embryo. He said each cell was already fixed.
challenging.against: In 1891 Hans Driesch separated sea urchin cells and each made a whole small sea urchin. Identical twins also grow from one ball that splits. Hilde Mangold's work, published in 1924, showed that neighbours change what cells become.

challenging.claim: Genes decide everything about a person.
challenging.who: Some people who read about DNA in the news.
challenging.for: Identical twins share all their genes and are often very alike in height and looks.
challenging.against: Identical twins have different fingerprints and sometimes different health. Children who are not fed well do not reach the height their genes allowed. Genes are instructions, and the surroundings change how they are used.

challenging.claim: The placenta is only a pipe that passes the mother's food to the baby.
challenging.for: Food and oxygen do pass from the mother to the baby through the placenta.
challenging.against: The placenta is also built by the baby's cells. It makes hormones, passes antibodies, removes the baby's waste, and keeps the two bloodstreams apart. It is an organ with several jobs, and not a pipe.

challenging.claim: Cells dying inside a body always means damage or disease.
challenging.for: Cells do die when we are hurt or ill.
challenging.against: Cells also die on purpose, on a signal, as part of building fingers, toes and many other parts. This is a normal and necessary part of growing.

challenging.claim: We only use ten percent of our brain.
challenging.who: A popular myth, often repeated in films.
challenging.for: Brain scans show that a few parts light up for each task, which can look like only a small part is used.
challenging.against: Scans show that over a day, nearly all parts of the brain are active. Damage to almost any part has a visible effect. Different tasks use different parts at different times.

big_questions.q: If every cell holds the same instructions, what makes a nerve cell different from a skin cell?
big_questions.hint: Think about the instructions, and about who or what each cell sits next to.

big_questions.q: Are cells what they are because of what is inside them, or because of where they are?
big_questions.hint: Remember what happened to piece 1 of the paper strip when the dye went in at the other end.

big_questions.q: If cells die on purpose so that you can have fingers, is dying a part of living?
big_questions.hint: Think about the tadpole's tail, a leaf falling, and the skin you lose every day.

big_questions.q: Before birth, the mother and the baby are fed through one meeting place. Are they one body, or two?
big_questions.hint: Their blood does not mix, but oxygen and food cross between them.

big_questions.q: A body is built with no builder standing outside it. Cells talk to cells, and a body appears. Who or what is making you?
big_questions.hint: Think about the signals, the instructions, the mother's food, and the cells themselves.

big_questions.q: Is a baby born ready, or made by what happens to them?
big_questions.hint: Think about a newborn's brain, which has many more connections than an adult's.

big_questions.q: Why does growing slow down? What would a person be like if growth never stopped?
big_questions.hint: Think about the growth plates, and about how tall a person could stand.

big_questions.q: Early cells take on the job of their new neighbours. Later cells keep their old job. Do people change in a similar way as they grow up?
big_questions.hint: Think about learning a language at three years old, and at thirty.

story.title: The Smell Map
story.note: A made-up story, set at a real kind of event, a big temple festival in Madurai. The science idea behind it is real. A smell, or any signal, gets weaker with distance from its source. Two such signals together can tell you exactly where you are. Cells in a growing embryo cannot smell, but they sense chemicals, and they use signals that fade with distance to find their place in the body.
text: Thenmozhi was nine, and she had never seen so many people in one place. It was the night of the big temple festival in Madurai. The streets around the temple were packed from wall to wall.
'Hold the end of my sari,' said her aunt, Selvi Athai. 'And listen to this rule. If we lose each other, do not wander. Go to the jasmine sellers at the east gate, and wait there. Say it back to me.'
'East gate. Jasmine sellers. Wait,' said Thenmozhi.

They walked past stalls of glass bangles and tiny drums, and a woman crushing sugarcane in a steel machine. Thenmozhi stopped to watch a man pulling hot sugar into long golden threads. Then drummers came through, with a crowd of dancers behind them. The crowd swelled and pushed. When she looked down, the end of the sari was gone from her hand.

'Athai!' she called. She could not even hear her own voice. The drums were too loud. She jumped up and down, but she saw only shoulders, elbows and bright paper flags. Every lane looked the same under the strings of lights.
Her heart was thumping. She remembered the rule. East gate. But which way was east? The sun had set hours ago. She turned in a slow circle, and every direction looked like every other.

Her teacher, Rani Miss, always said that when you are frightened, you should stop and breathe slowly three times. Thenmozhi stood very still with her back against a pillar, and breathed in, and out, three times. On the third breath, she noticed her nose.
The air smelled strongly of hot oil and chillies. That was the vadai stall right beside her. Under it there was a very faint sweetness, cool and soft. It was jasmine.

She remembered coming in. At the east gate, the jasmine had been so thick that she had closed her eyes. As they had walked deeper into the crowd, the jasmine had faded, and the smell of frying had taken over. 'Strong jasmine means the gate,' she thought. 'Strong frying means the middle. And now there is strong frying and only a tiny bit of jasmine. So I am in the middle, a long way from the gate.'

But which way was the gate? She tried a few steps to her left. She sniffed. The frying smell was just as strong, but the jasmine was fainter. That was the wrong way. She turned around and tried the other side. The jasmine was a little stronger there, and the frying smell a little weaker.

She began to walk. At every few steps she asked herself the same two questions. Is the jasmine getting stronger? Is the frying getting weaker? When the answer was yes, she kept going. When the answer was no, she stopped and turned. A man tried to hurry her along, but she kept her place at the edge of the lane, close to the shop walls, where it was safe.

The frying smell faded. A cool smell of flowers took its place, and it grew stronger, step after step. Soon it was so strong that the whole air tasted sweet. She looked up. Ropes of white jasmine hung from a great stone arch, and beneath them sat a row of women with baskets of flowers.
Under the arch stood Selvi Athai. Her face was pale and her hair had come loose. She saw Thenmozhi and ran, and held her so tightly that Thenmozhi could hardly breathe.
'I looked in every lane!' said Athai. 'How did you find the gate? You could not see over the crowd.'

'I smelled it,' said Thenmozhi. 'The jasmine was strong at the gate and weak in the middle. The frying was strong in the middle and weak at the gate. So with both smells, I knew where I was.' She stopped. 'I did not know the way. But the smells did.'
The flower seller, Mallika Akka, laughed and gave her a small string of jasmine for her hair. 'Good nose,' she said. 'Our jasmine has led many lost people home.'

That night, Thenmozhi lay on the roof of her cousin's house, with the jasmine in her hair and the festival lights still glowing in the sky. She thought about the two smells, the strong and the weak. She had no map and no name board. She had only how much of each smell reached her nose. And that had been enough to tell her exactly where she stood.
story.epiphany: A smell gets weaker with distance from its source. Because of that, how strong it is tells you how far away you are, and two smells together tell you where you stand.
ask: A smell fades as you walk away. How can a fading smell tell you how far away its source is?
Why did Thenmozhi need two smells and not just one?
Cells in an embryo cannot see or hear. What could they use, instead of smell, to find out where they are?
art: A girl in a green skirt holding the end of a sari in a packed lane of a Madurai temple festival, with strings of lights and a stall frying vadai.
The same girl alone, her hand empty, surrounded by a forest of shoulders and flags, with drummers disappearing behind her.
The girl with her back to a stone pillar, eyes closed, taking a slow breath, with faint swirls of oil smoke on one side and jasmine on the other.
A stone gate hung with white jasmine ropes, women with flower baskets below, and an aunt hugging the girl.

roots.context: We have followed how one cell becomes a whole body, and how cells find their jobs. Now we ask what this says about who builds a body, and who we are.

deep_truth.truth: Nearly every cell in your body holds the same instructions. Yet one becomes bone and another becomes skin, depending on where each one sits. A signal fades with distance, so cells can tell their place from how much has reached them. Cells get their jobs from their neighbours, not from a stamp inside.
deep_truth.habit: We picture a body as built from a blueprint, with every part given out in advance, and we picture cells as carrying their own labels, such as 'I am a nerve cell'. But in an early embryo, the job depends on the place and the neighbours.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Colour Map test, the same spot on a paper strip came out dark when the dye went in at one end, and pale when it went in at the other. In work published in 1924, Hilde Mangold moved a small piece of newt embryo and the cells around it started to build a second body. The paper is only a model, but the two results point the same way.

three.who_am_i: You are a community of about 30 trillion cells that hold the same instructions, and each cell found their job by listening to their neighbours.
three.what_is_life: A living body builds itself. Cells talk to cells, with no builder standing outside, and a hand, a heart and a brain appear.
three.what_is_this_world: A pattern can come from one smooth change, like a colour fading along a strip, and nobody has to draw each part.

roots.thread: One cell holds all the instructions. It splits, and the new cells hold them too. Then, with the help of signals, one set of instructions becomes more than 200 kinds of cell, in the right places. The One turns into the many without anything leaving the whole. Cells that began as one remain connected by the signals they pass. The fingers, the heart and the brain are all one growing thing, made of one family of cells.

teachings.teaching: A father, Uddalaka, asks his son Shvetaketu to break open a fruit of the banyan tree, and then to break open one of its tiny seeds. 'What do you see?' 'Nothing, sir.' The father says that from this unseen essence, a great banyan tree grows.
teachings.link: A fertilised egg is too small to see, and no tree or body is visible inside it. Yet it holds the instructions for a whole person. Something unseen carries everything that will grow.

teachings.teaching: 'The Tao gives birth to One. One gives birth to Two. Two gives birth to Three. Three gives birth to all things.'
teachings.link: One cell makes two, then four, then trillions. From a single start come hundreds of kinds of cell, and a whole body.

teachings.source: Fazang's Treatise on the Golden Lion (about 700 CE), using the Hua-yen image of Indra's net
teachings.teaching: Fazang, a Chinese Buddhist teacher, described a net of jewels in which every jewel reflects all the other jewels. Each one holds the whole net inside it.
teachings.link: In an embryo, every cell holds the whole set of instructions, and each cell's job depends on every cell around them.

science.text: Animals from flies to mice to people use signals that fade with distance to tell cells where they are, and the same families of signals are used again and again.
How the cells of a growing body know when to stop, so that each organ ends up the right size, is not fully understood.

other_view.view: A cell does not read, decide or know anything. A signal binds to a molecule on the cell's surface, and that sets off a chain of chemical changes that switch certain genes on. 'Reading a signal' is only a way of speaking about chemistry.

practice.title: Feel the warmth fade
practice.say: Hold your palms facing each other, about one finger-width apart. Breathe slowly three times. Feel the warmth between your palms. Now slowly move them apart, about one finger-width at a time. Notice where the warmth gets weaker and where you stop feeling it. Then bring your hands back together, slowly, and notice the warmth return.
practice.kid: Hold your palms facing each other. Feel the warmth between them. Slowly move them apart. Where does the warmth fade? Bring them back.

ask: If cells get their jobs from their neighbours, are they still the same cells they were before?
Where in you does 'you' get decided: inside each cell, or between the cells?
Two cells hold the same instructions, and become different. What made them different?
roots.art: A cluster of cells with warm glows passing between neighbours, one cell at the centre lit brightest and the others shaded by distance, over a faint outline of a child's hand.

games.title: Timeline Detective: what comes first?
games.context: This is a card game about when things happen in growing. You put events in order along a timeline, from one cell to the teens.

setup.art: Twenty-two cards on a table, with one card lying face-up in the middle as the start of a timeline.
setup.caption: 1. Shuffle the cards. Put one face-up in the middle with its time showing.

setup.art: A player holding a card and placing it between two cards on the timeline.
setup.caption: 2. Take a card. Place it where you think it belongs in the line.

setup.art: The new card turned over, showing its time, with two neighbour cards showing theirs.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the card over. Is it in the right place?

printables.title: 22 two-sided cards: an event on the front, and when it happens on the back

items.f: One cell begins
items.b: Day 1. A single new cell holds a full set of instructions.

items.f: A ball of about 100 cells
items.b: Day 5. The cell has split again and again into a small hollow ball.

items.f: The ball settles into the womb wall
items.b: Week 2. The placenta begins to form here.

items.f: The heart starts to beat
items.b: Week 3. A tiny tube of cells begins to pulse.

items.f: A flat strip of cells rolls into a tube that will become brain and spine
items.b: Week 4. The tube closes.

items.f: Small buds show where arms and legs will grow
items.b: Week 5. The buds are smaller than a grain of rice.

items.f: The fingers separate as the cells between them die
items.b: Week 8. A flat paddle becomes a hand.

items.f: The baby is now called a foetus
items.b: Week 9. All the main parts have begun, and the baby mostly grows.

items.f: The mother may feel the first small flutters
items.b: About week 17. The baby's movements are strong enough to feel. Some mothers feel them earlier or later.

items.f: The baby is born
items.b: Week 38 of growing. This is about week 40 of pregnancy.

items.f: The cord stump falls off, leaving the belly button
items.b: About 10 days after birth. It happens a few days earlier or later.

items.f: A first real smile at another person
items.b: About 6 weeks old. Some babies smile a little earlier or later.

items.f: Holds the head steady when held upright
items.b: About 4 months old.

items.f: Rolls from front to back
items.b: About 5 months old.

items.f: Sits without help
items.b: About 6 months old. Babies vary by a month or two.

items.f: Walks while holding on to furniture
items.b: About 9 months old.

items.f: Stands alone for a moment
items.b: About 11 months old.

items.f: Takes first steps alone
items.b: About 12 months old. Many babies walk between 9 and 17 months.

items.f: Puts two words together
items.b: About 2 years old.

items.f: All 20 milk teeth have come
items.b: About 3 years old.

items.f: The first milk tooth falls out
items.b: About 6 years old.

items.f: The growth spurt of the early teens begins
items.b: Girls about 10 to 11 years old, boys about 12 to 13.

rules: The goal is to place cards in the right order on a timeline. The timeline runs from the earliest event on the left to the latest on the right.
Turn the whole pile over. Take the top card and place it face-up in the middle of the table, with its back (the time) showing. This is the start of the timeline.
On your turn, take the top card from the pile. Read the front aloud. Do not look at the back.
Place it face-up in the timeline where you think it belongs. It can go to the left of the line, between two cards, or to the right. Cards in the line show their back.

Turn your card over to show its back, and look at the times. If your card sits in a correct place, between a card that is earlier or at the same time and a card that is later or at the same time, it stays in the line, and you score one point.
If it is in the wrong place, move it to the right place, and score no points. Where times are about equal, either order is fine.
The game ends when the pile is empty. The player with the most points wins. If you play alone, count your points out of 21. Try to beat your own score next time.
Babies differ. The times on the cards are typical times, and a healthy baby can be a few weeks or months earlier or later.

flow.do: Cut out the 22 cards. Shuffle them and make a pile with the fronts facing up. Turn the top card over. Place it in the middle of the table with its back showing. Read the back aloud.
flow.say: These cards show things that happen as a person grows. Each card has an event on one side and the time on the other. We will put them in order. Here is the first one.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Shuffle them. Turn the top card over and put it in the middle.
flow.context: This is the first step of Timeline Detective. You set up the cards.

flow.do: Play six turns. After each, read the back aloud. After the third card, ask the question below.
flow.say: Take a card. Read it aloud. Where does it go in the line? Place it, then turn it over to check.
flow.kid: Take a card. Read it. Place it in the line. Turn it over and check.

ask.q: Which event surprised you the most, and why?
good: The fingers separating by week eight.
So many things happen before birth.

flow.parent: The first nine cards happen before birth. Most children are surprised by how early the heart begins to beat, at about three weeks. Check any 'week' against the back of the card.
flow.context: In this step, you play the first turns and learn how the line works.

flow.do: Play the next eight turns. Keep the points on paper. If you are playing alone, keep a tally of right placements.
flow.say: Keep going. Think about what a baby can do just after they are born, and what comes later. Which comes first, sitting or standing?
flow.kid: Keep playing. Which comes first, sitting or standing?

ask.q: Which events happen before birth, and which after?
good: Heart, hands and buds are before birth.
Smiling and sitting are after birth.

flow.context: In this step, you play the middle of the game and keep score.

flow.do: Play the last cards. When the pile is finished, count the points. Look at the timeline from left to right.
flow.say: Last cards. Place them carefully. Then count your points.
flow.kid: Play the last cards. Count your points.
flow.context: In this step, you finish the pile and count the points.

flow.do: Read the whole timeline aloud, from left to right. Ask your child where growth was fastest and which card they would change.
flow.say: Read the timeline from the start to the end. Where do many things happen close together? Where are the long gaps?
flow.kid: Read the timeline. Where do many things happen close together? Where are the long gaps?
flow.parent: Many events are crowded in the first eight weeks, when the main parts of the body are laid down. After that, they mostly grow and learn. The long gaps later show that learning to move and speak takes much longer than building the body.
flow.think: Most of the building of the body happens in the first eight weeks. Why do you think it takes years to learn to run?
flow.context: This is the last step of Timeline Detective. You look back at the whole line.

experiments.title: Colour Map: how can cells know where they are?
experiments.question: A strip of paper is dipped in dye at one end. Can you tell where you are on the strip just from the colour? And what happens to each piece's 'job' if the dye goes in at the other end?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. After the dye has travelled along the strip, will the colour be the same all along, or different? What will happen if the dye goes in at the other end? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Both strips are cut from the same paper towel. They have the same width and length. Each has the same dye, the same depth of dye in the same kind of katori, and the same time. Only the end that touches the dye is different. So any difference between the two strips comes from which end got the dye.
results_table: Strip A, dye at the left: colour
Strip B, dye at the right: colour

materials.item: 2 strips cut from a white kitchen paper towel, each 3 centimetres wide and 18 centimetres long (a coffee filter paper cut into strips also works)
red or blue food colour, 10 drops (or a tablespoon of strong beetroot water)
2 small steel katoris or cups, with 3 tablespoons of water in each
a pencil, a ruler and a pair of scissors
a clean plastic tray or a large plate
a timer or clock, and the results table

experiments.safety: Food colour stains clothes, hands and table tops. Put the tray on newspaper. Do not drink or taste anything in the katoris. Use the scissors with a grown-up nearby. Wash your hands afterwards.
experiments.record: Write the colour of each piece, dark, medium, pale or none, for strip A and for strip B. Then give each piece a made-up job: dark is bone, medium is muscle, pale is skin, and none is waiting.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you make a model of how cells in an embryo can find their jobs. You do it with dye on paper.

setup.art: A paper strip lying on a tray, with pencil lines every 3 centimetres making six squares, numbered 1 to 6 from the left.
setup.caption: 1. Cut two strips. Draw 5 lines to make 6 pieces. Number them 1 to 6 from the left.

setup.art: Two steel katoris of red-dyed water, one at the left end of the tray and one at the right end, with a ruler between them.
setup.caption: 2. Put 10 drops of colour in each katori of water. Place one katori at each end of the tray.

setup.art: Strip A with its left end folded over the rim of the left katori, dipping 1 centimetre into the dye, and strip B with its right end dipping into the right katori.
setup.caption: 3. Strip A dips in at its left end. Strip B dips in at its right end.

setup.art: The two strips after a few minutes, each dark near its dipped end and fading to pale at the far end.
setup.caption: 4. Watch the dye climb. Lift strip A when its front reaches piece 5, and strip B when its front reaches piece 2.

setup.art: Each strip cut into six pieces laid in a row, with a small label under each piece: bone, muscle, skin or waiting.
setup.caption: 5. Look at each piece. Write its colour, then its made-up job.

flow.do: Show your child the paper strips and the dye. Explain that they will make a model of cells in an embryo. Each piece of paper is a cell, and the dye is a signal. Ask for a guess and a reason, and write both down.
flow.say: Each piece of this strip is like a cell in a growing body. The dye is like a signal. Will the colour be the same along the whole strip? What if the dye goes in at the other end? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Each paper piece is like a cell. The dye is like a signal. Will the colour be the same all along? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think the colour will look like that?
good: The dye gets weaker as it goes.
It will be dark where it starts.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start. Tell them this is only a model, because real cells use chemical signals and not dye.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Colour Map test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Cut two strips, each 3 centimetres wide and 18 centimetres long. Draw five pencil lines across each strip, 3 centimetres apart, to make six pieces. Number the pieces 1 to 6 from the left, on both strips. Stir 10 drops of colour into each katori.
flow.say: Cut two strips of paper towel. Draw lines to make six pieces on each. Number the pieces from the left, one to six. Stir the colour into the water.
flow.kid: Cut two strips. Draw five lines to make six pieces. Number the pieces 1 to 6. Stir colour into the water.
flow.parent: If the dye is too strong, the whole strip will turn dark. A first test is a good guide. Begin with 10 drops in 3 tablespoons of water. You can add water later if the dye is too dark.

check.q: Why do we cut both strips from the same paper towel and make them the same size?
options: So the only difference is which end touches the dye
So the strips look the same
check.why: If the strips were different, a difference in the pattern could come from the paper, and not from the dye. We change one thing only, which end gets the dye.

flow.context: In this step, you prepare the strips and the dye. Both strips must be the same.

flow.do: Place a katori at each end of the tray. Fold the left end of strip A over the left katori so that 1 centimetre dips into the dye. Fold the right end of strip B over the right katori in the same way. Keep the two strips apart so they do not touch. Set a timer. Watch the dye climb. Lift strip A out when its front reaches piece 5. Lift strip B out when its front reaches piece 2, which is the same distance from its dye. Lay both on the tray.
flow.say: Strip A dips in at the left. Strip B dips in at the right. Start the timer and watch the dye climb. Lift strip A when the dye reaches piece five. Lift strip B when the dye reaches piece two. Then both have travelled the same distance.
flow.kid: Dip strip A at its left end. Dip strip B at its right end. Watch the dye climb. Lift A at piece 5. Lift B at piece 2.

ask.q: What do you see where the dye has not yet reached?
good: The front is a pale line.

flow.parent: Dye takes about 5 to 20 minutes to climb 12 to 15 centimetres, depending on the paper. Use the front as your clock, not the timer. If the whole strip is dark and the same, the dye is too strong. Add the same amount of water to the katori and try again with a new strip. That is a result too. If the whole strip is pale, add a few more drops.

check.q: The dye is darkest near the katori and faint at the far end of the strip. What does this show?
options: The amount of dye falls as you move away from where it went in
The paper is darker at one end
The dye is stuck at the start
check.why: The colour changes smoothly from dark to pale along the strip. The amount of dye falls with distance from the source. That is what a gradient is.

flow.context: In this step, you start the signal and watch it spread. You stop it before it reaches the far end.

flow.do: Lay the two strips side by side on the tray, with piece 1 on the left on both. For each piece write its colour. Then give each piece its made-up job. Dark is bone, medium is muscle, pale is skin, and no colour is waiting. Cut each strip into its six pieces and lay them in rows.
flow.say: Look at each piece. Is it dark, medium, pale, or white? Write it down. Then give each piece a job. Dark is bone, medium is muscle, pale is skin, and white is waiting.
flow.kid: Look at each piece. Write its colour. Dark is bone. Medium is muscle. Pale is skin. White is waiting.
flow.parent: The jobs are made up, to show the idea. A real embryo uses chemical signals, and many more jobs. Look for a smooth change from dark to pale along each strip.
flow.context: In this step, you read the colour of each piece and give it a job, like a cell reading a signal.

flow.do: Pick up piece 1 from strip A and piece 1 from strip B. Ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw, and why. Then ask what would happen with a third strip, dipped in the middle.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did you see? Why do you think it happened? Look at the two piece ones. They are the same paper. Why do they have different jobs?
flow.kid: Hold piece 1 of each strip. Same paper, but different jobs. Say what you thought, what you saw, and why.

ask.q: What would happen to the pieces if the dye went into the middle of a strip?
good: Pieces near the middle are dark and the ends are pale.

flow.parent: A strong answer says that piece 1 got the job its colour showed. It was dark when it was next to the dye, and pale or white when it was far from the dye. Nothing about the paper changed. Where it sat decided the job. After they have said what they saw, explain: a real embryo uses chemical signals that spread and fade in the same way. A cell reads how much has reached them, and so learns where they are. Cut a third strip and dip it in the middle if there is time. The pattern is a mirror. That is how symmetric parts of a body can be made from one signal.
flow.think: Real cells in an embryo cannot see colour. What could cells use, instead of colour, to find out where they are?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Colour Map test. You say your claim, your evidence and your reasoning.

experiments.title: Wrong-Hand Writing: how fast does practice work?
experiments.question: If you write the same short line with the hand you do not usually use, six times in a row, how much faster do you get? Does each try save the same amount of time?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. How many seconds will your first try take? Will your sixth try be faster, and by how much? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: You write the same line, on the same kind of paper, with the same pen, sitting the same way. You rest for one minute between tries. Only the try number changes. So if the times get shorter, practice is the only thing that can have changed.
results_table: Seconds saved since the last try

materials.item: a pen or pencil
7 sheets of plain paper, or a notebook with 7 clean lines
a timer, a phone or a clock with a seconds hand
a helper to time and to say start and stop
graph paper or squared paper, and the results table

experiments.record: Write the time for each try in the results table. Work out the seconds saved since the last try. Then draw a line graph of time against try number.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you find out how fast practice changes how well you can do something new. You write a short line with the hand you do not usually use.

setup.art: A child sitting at a table writing with their left hand, while a parent holds a clock and watches.
setup.caption: 1. Sit the same way each time. A helper watches the clock.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with the line 'I am growing' written wobbly with the wrong hand, and a clock beside it showing seconds.
setup.caption: 2. Write the same line on a new line each time. Your helper times you.

setup.art: A results table with six rows of times, going down from the first to the sixth.
setup.caption: 3. Write each time in the table. Rest for a minute between tries.

setup.art: A line graph with six points joined, starting high at try 1 and flattening at the right.
setup.caption: 4. Draw a line graph of time against try number.

flow.do: Show your child the line to write. The line is I am growing today. Ask them to guess the time of the first try, and of the sixth try. Ask for a reason, and write the guesses down.
flow.say: We will write the same line six times with your other hand. How long do you think the first try will take? And the sixth? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: You will write a line six times with your other hand. Guess your first time and your last time. Why?

ask.q: Why do you think the sixth try will be faster or slower?
good: I will get used to it.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Use the same line each time, 'I am growing today', so the amount of writing does not change.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Wrong-Hand test. You guess before you start.

flow.do: Ask your child to write the line once with their usual hand. Time it and write down the number. This is their best possible time, to compare with.
flow.say: First, write the line with your usual hand. Go. Stop. That time is your comparison.
flow.kid: Write the line with your usual hand. Your helper times it.
flow.context: In this step, you time the usual hand, so you have a comparison.

flow.do: Now they write the line with the other hand, six times, on a new line each time. Time each try. Write each time in the results table. Between tries, rest for one minute with the pen down.
flow.say: Now use your other hand. Ready, go. Stop. Write down the time. Now rest for one minute. Then try again.
flow.kid: Use your other hand. Write the line. Your helper times it. Rest for a minute. Do this six times.

ask.q: Which part of your hand or your head feels different on the sixth try?
good: I do not have to think about each letter.

flow.parent: Stay calm and do not hurry them. Do not let them look at earlier tries. If a time goes up, write it down. That is a result too. Tiredness can slow the later tries.

check.q: On the fourth try your child takes 3 seconds longer than on the third. What is the best way to treat this result?
options: Write it down as it is and keep going
Cross it out and do it again
check.why: A real result is written down even when it is surprising. One slow try can come from tiredness, and the pattern over all six tries is what counts.

flow.context: In this step, you do the six tries and record each time.

flow.do: Work out the seconds saved on each try. Then draw a line graph with the try number along the bottom and the time up the side. Join the points.
flow.say: For each try, take away this time from the last time. That gives the seconds saved. Now draw a line graph. Try number goes along the bottom. Time goes up the side.
flow.kid: Work out the seconds saved on each try. Draw a line graph. Join the points.
flow.context: In this step, you turn the numbers into a line graph and look at its shape.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw, and why. Ask which try saved the most time.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think? What did you see? Why do you think the times changed? Which try saved the most time?
flow.kid: Say what you thought, what you saw, and why. Which try saved the most?
flow.parent: Most people save the most time in the first two or three tries, and then the line flattens. After they have said what they saw, explain: each time you write, the connections between nerve cells that you use get stronger, so the movement needs less effort. The line flattens because the easy gains come first. If there is time, try again tomorrow. The first try tomorrow is often still faster than today's first try.
flow.think: If you practised for a week, what would the line look like at the end?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Wrong-Hand test. You say your claim, your evidence and your reasoning.

activities.title: A Hand Made by Taking Away

materials.item: a ball of atta dough, about the size of a fist (or clay)
a rolling pin (belan), or a clean bottle
a blunt plastic knife or a butter knife
a pencil

activities.safety: Do not eat the raw dough. Use a blunt knife with a grown-up nearby. Atta contains wheat, so if anyone in the family is allergic to wheat or gluten, use clay or play dough instead. Wash your hands afterwards.
activities.record: Draw your two finished hands and write which was easier, and why.
activities.context: In this activity, you model how a hand forms, by taking dough away. You find out why a hand does not grow by adding fingers.

setup.art: A child rolling a ball of dough into a flat oval paddle with a rolling pin.
setup.caption: 1. Roll the dough into a flat paddle, about as thick as your finger.

setup.art: The dough paddle with four pencil lines drawn from the top edge down to two-thirds of the way.
setup.caption: 2. Draw 4 lines from the top edge, to make 5 finger shapes.

setup.art: A hand of dough with gaps between the fingers, and the cut-away dough pieces beside it.
setup.caption: 3. Cut away the dough between the lines, with a blunt knife.

flow.do: Roll the dough flat into an oval paddle, as thick as your finger and as long as your hand. Show your child their own hand with the fingers pressed together. Say that a hand started like this.
flow.say: Your hand began as a flat paddle like this one. Look at your own hand with your fingers pressed together. How do you think a paddle becomes five fingers?
flow.kid: Roll the dough into a flat paddle. Press your fingers together. How does a paddle become five fingers?

ask.q: How do you think the paddle becomes five fingers?
good: Cells grow out from the paddle.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess is fine. Show them the paddle shape in your own hand with the fingers together.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Hand activity. You roll a paddle and guess how it becomes a hand.

flow.do: Draw four lines from the top of the paddle down two-thirds of the way. Cut away the dough between the lines, with a blunt knife. Pull the cut pieces away. Then make a second hand from a new paddle by rolling five little fingers and sticking them on. Compare the two hands.
flow.say: Draw four lines from the top. Cut out the dough between the lines. Take the pieces away. Now try a second hand. Roll five little fingers and stick them on. Which hand is better?
flow.kid: Cut the dough between the lines to make fingers. Make a second hand by sticking five fingers on. Compare.
flow.parent: The cut hand has fingers that are joined to the palm all the way. The stuck-on fingers may fall off. In a real embryo, the fingers do not stick on. They appear when the cells between them die on a signal.

check.q: In an embryo, what makes the gaps between the fingers?
options: Cells between the fingers die when they get a signal
Fingers grow out and stick on to the palm
The hand is cut by the womb
check.why: The hand begins as a flat paddle. A signal tells the cells between the finger lines to die, and that leaves the fingers. Nothing is stuck on and nothing cuts.

flow.context: In this step, you make one hand by taking dough away, and one hand by adding fingers.

flow.do: Look at the web of skin at the base of your own fingers. Spread your fingers wide. Talk about ducks, who have webbed feet. Ask what might be different in a duck's foot.
flow.say: Look at the small web of skin between your fingers at the bottom. A duck has much more web between their toes. What might be different in a duck's foot while it grows?
flow.kid: Spread your fingers wide. Look at the web at the bottom. A duck has more web. Why?

ask.q: What might be different in a duck's foot while it grows?
good: Fewer cells die between the toes.

flow.parent: In a chick, the cells between the toes die and the toes are separate. In a duck, most of those cells stay alive, so the toes stay webbed. After they have shared their idea, say so. In a few babies, two fingers stay joined, and a small operation separates them.
flow.think: Which is the better shape for swimming, a hand with webbing or a hand without?
flow.context: In this step, you compare your hand with a duck's foot.

activities.title: My Growth Line: how fast does a baby grow?

materials.item: squared paper or graph paper
a pencil and a ruler
the baby health card that your family has, if you have one (in India it is often called the Mother and Child Protection card)

activities.record: Draw a line graph of a baby's length from birth to 2 years. Mark the steepest part.
activities.context: In this activity, you draw a line graph of how a baby's length grows in the first two years, from typical values measured in thousands of healthy babies.

setup.art: A sheet of squared paper with a horizontal axis marked 0 to 24 months and a vertical axis marked 40 to 90 centimetres.
setup.caption: 1. Draw the axes. Months along the bottom, length up the side.

setup.art: Six dots on the grid at 0, 3, 6, 9, 12 and 24 months, rising from left to right.
setup.caption: 2. Mark a dot for each age and length from the table.

setup.art: The dots joined by a line, with the steepest part near the start marked by a bracket.
setup.caption: 3. Join the dots. Mark the steepest part.

flow.do: Show your child the typical lengths for a healthy baby. At birth the baby is 50 centimetres long. Then 61 at 3 months, 67 at 6 months, 71 at 9 months, 75 at 12 months, and 87 at 24 months. Ask in which three months a baby grows the most, and why they think so.
flow.say: Here are typical lengths for a healthy baby. At birth, 50 centimetres. At three months, 61. At six months, 67. At nine months, 71. At twelve months, 75. At two years, 87. In which three months does a baby grow the most? Why?
flow.kid: Here are baby lengths. 50, 61, 67, 71, 75, 87 centimetres. When does a baby grow most? Why?

ask.q: When do you think a baby grows fastest?

flow.parent: These are typical middle values from the World Health Organization growth standards, rounded. Real babies are a little above or below. Do not correct the guess.
flow.context: This is the first step of My Growth Line. You guess when growth is fastest.

flow.do: Draw the axes. Put months along the bottom, from 0 to 24, and length up the side, from 40 to 90 centimetres. Mark a dot for each age and length. Join the dots with a ruler.
flow.say: Draw the axes on the squared paper. Months go along the bottom. Length goes up the side. Mark a dot for each age. Then join the dots with a ruler.
flow.kid: Draw the axes. Mark a dot for each age. Join the dots.
flow.parent: If you have a baby health card, you can plot your own child's first two years in a second colour. Different babies follow their own line. A baby who is steady on their own line is growing well.
flow.context: In this step, you draw the line graph.

flow.do: Work out how many centimetres were gained in each step. Mark the steepest part of the line. Ask what the line would look like at age 5, and at age 12.
flow.say: How many centimetres were gained in each step? Which step is the steepest? The line goes up at the start and then flattens. Why do you think growth slows?
flow.kid: Find the steepest part. Count how much was gained in each step. Why does growth slow?

ask.q: What do you think the line will look like at 5 years old?
good: It will keep going up, but slowly.
It will go up in steps.

flow.parent: Gains in length: 11 centimetres in the first three months, 6 in the next three, 4 in the next three, 4 in the next, and 12 in the whole second year. The line is steepest at the start. After they have made their own claim, explain: a baby grows fastest in the womb and just after birth, and then more slowly. Growth speeds up again in the early teens. Never compare your child to another child. Compare them to their own line.
flow.think: If a baby kept growing 11 centimetres every three months, how tall would they be at 10 years old?
flow.context: In this step, you read the graph and say when growth is fastest.

activities.title: Same Book, Different Pages

materials.item: 2 sheets of paper, each with the same 8 instruction lines written on them (see the first step)
4 small slips of paper with signal words written on them
2 pencils or crayons of different colours

activities.record: Keep the two marked instruction sheets. Write which lines were different for each cell.
activities.context: In this activity, you act out how two cells hold the same instructions but use different ones. One person is a hair cell and one is a red blood cell.

setup.art: Two identical sheets of paper, each headed 'Instruction book' and listing the same 8 lines.
setup.caption: 1. Write the same 8 lines on both sheets.

setup.art: A slip of paper reading 'You are in the scalp' held up beside a sheet.
setup.caption: 2. A neighbour shows a signal slip to each cell.

setup.art: Two marked sheets side by side, each with different lines circled.
setup.caption: 3. Each cell circles the lines they follow.

flow.do: Write these 8 lines on both sheets. Line 1: make keratin, the hair and nail protein. Line 2: make haemoglobin, which carries oxygen. Line 3: make collagen, the tough protein in skin and bone. Line 4: make muscle fibres. Line 5: make lens protein, which is clear. Line 6: make a gut enzyme to break down food. Line 7: make signals for a nerve. Line 8: make energy and repair parts.
flow.say: We will write one instruction book with eight lines, and make two copies. Each copy is the DNA of a cell. Every cell gets the whole book.
flow.kid: Write eight lines on a sheet. Make a second copy. Every cell gets a whole book.
flow.parent: The lines are simple, made-up examples of real jobs. A real cell reads a code written in four chemical letters, not lines of words.
flow.context: This is the first step of Same Book, Different Pages. You make two copies of one book of instructions.

flow.do: Your child is cell A and you are cell B. Read a signal slip to each cell. Cell A gets the slip 'You are in the scalp'. Cell B gets 'You are in the bone marrow'. Each cell circles line 8, and the line the signal points to. A scalp cell follows line 1. A bone marrow cell follows line 2.
flow.say: You are cell A and I am cell B. We both have the whole book. Now I read your signal. You are in the scalp. Circle the lines a hair cell follows. Remember line eight. Every cell follows line eight.
flow.kid: Each cell gets a signal. Circle line 8, and the lines your signal tells you to follow.

ask.q: Which lines did both cells follow? Which lines were different?

flow.parent: Line 8 is what every cell needs. The other lines are the special jobs. Try a second round with new signals, such as 'You are in the lens of the eye' and 'You are in the gut'. The books never change. Only the circled lines change.
flow.context: In this step, each cell gets a signal and circles the lines to follow.

flow.do: Compare the two sheets. Ask your child how the books differ and how the marking differs. Then ask who decided which lines to follow.
flow.say: Look at the two books. Are they the same? Look at the circled lines. Are they the same? Who decided which lines to follow?
flow.kid: Compare the two books. Compare the circles. Who decided which lines to follow?
flow.parent: The books are identical. The marked lines are different, and the signals came from the neighbours. In early embryos, moved cells follow the signals of their new place. After they have shared their idea, say so. Later in development, cells settle and keep their job.
flow.think: If a cell in your skin were moved to your eye early in life, which lines would they follow?
flow.context: In this step, you compare the books and the marks.

projects.title: Family Growth Interviews: when did you grow?

materials.item: a notebook and a pencil
a tape measure or a ruler
two or three family members, such as parents, grandparents, an uncle or an aunt, who are happy to be interviewed

schedule.what: Write the five questions. Interview your first family member and write their answers.
Interview two more family members. Measure everyone's height today.
Draw a growth line for each person. Compare them. Write what you found.

projects.record: Draw one growth line for each person you interviewed, with at least three dots for their height at different ages. Write one thing that is the same, and one thing that is different.
projects.context: In this project, you interview family members about how and when they grew. You draw a growth line for each and compare them with the growth line of a baby.

setup.art: A child with a notebook, interviewing a grandmother sitting on a sofa.
setup.caption: 1. Ask your family member five questions. Write down their answers.

setup.art: A tape measure held against a door frame beside an adult standing straight.
setup.caption: 2. Measure each person's height today.

setup.art: Three growth lines drawn on one sheet of squared paper in three colours.
setup.caption: 3. Draw a growth line for each person. Compare them.

flow.do: Write these questions in the notebook. When were you born, and how long were you? How tall were you at 10? When did you grow the fastest? When did you stop growing? What are you good at now, that you needed to practise? Ask the first family member and write their answers.
flow.say: We will ask family members about their growth. Here are five questions. Write them in your notebook. Then ask the first person. Be kind, and ask only what they want to share.
flow.kid: Write five questions. Ask your first family member. Write down their answers.

ask.q: Whom would you like to interview first, and why?

flow.parent: Some people may not remember their birth length or height at 10. That is fine. Ask them to guess, or skip the question. Growth is a private topic for some people. Ask only what they are happy to share. Not everyone grew up with their parents, and some children have no family record. Pick anyone who cares for you.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Family Growth Interviews. You prepare the questions and ask the first person.

flow.do: Interview two more family members. Measure everyone's height today. Write each person's answers next to their name.
flow.say: Today we ask two more people the same five questions. Then we measure everyone with the tape. Write it all next to their names.
flow.kid: Interview two more people. Measure everyone's height. Write it down.
flow.context: In this step, you interview two more family members and measure everyone's height.

flow.do: For each person, draw a growth line on squared paper, with age along the bottom and height up the side. Mark at least three dots. Join them. Compare the lines with each other and with the baby's growth line from the Growth Line activity.
flow.say: Draw a growth line for each person, with age along the bottom and height up the side. Join the dots. What is the same in every line? What is different?
flow.kid: Draw a growth line for each person. What is the same in every line? What is different?

ask.q: What is the same in all the lines?
good: They all go up and then flatten.
Everyone stopped growing at some age.
Everyone grew fast when they were young.

flow.parent: Most people say they grew fastest as a young child, and again in the early teens. Girls usually stop growing earlier than boys, in the middle to late teens. After they have shared what they found, explain: the growth plates close, and the bones cannot grow longer.
flow.think: Why might the lines stop at different heights and different ages?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Family Growth Interviews. You draw and compare the lines.

challenges.title: Three Stripes From One Dye
challenges.problem: You have only one bottle of dye and one kind of paper towel. Make a strip of paper that shows three clear bands, dark, medium and pale, so that a stranger could tell which band is which at a glance. You may not paint or colour the strip with a brush or a pen.
challenges.safety: Food colour stains clothes, hands and table tops. Put the tray on newspaper. Use the scissors with a grown-up nearby. Do not taste anything. Wash your hands afterwards.
constraints: Use only one colour of dye.
Do not paint or draw on the strip.
The three bands must be clearly different from each other.
Test your idea and keep your results.
materials: paper towel or coffee filter strips
general: Dip one end of a strip in dye for a short time, then cut it into three pieces. The ends will have dark, medium and pale colours. Tape them together.
Make three katoris with different amounts of dye, such as 12, 6 and 3 drops in the same amount of water. Dip a short strip in each, and tape the three strips together in order.
Dip one end in dye and stop when the front reaches the middle. The strip will fade from dark to pale.
creative: Fold a strip in three and dip each fold to a different depth.
Dip both ends to make a pale middle and two dark ends, then use the three parts as bands.
Make a staircase: dip a long strip, move it a little each minute, and see what stripes appear.
challenges.your_turn: Try two of the ideas on small strips. Choose the one that gives the clearest three bands. Then ask someone who has not seen your strips to say which band is dark, medium and pale. If they can, your design works.
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about gradients. You use one dye and make three clear bands, the way a growing embryo makes different cells from one signal.

setup.art: Three small katoris of red dye, from deep red to pale pink, with three paper strips dipping in them.
setup.caption: 1. One idea: three katoris with strong, medium and weak dye.

setup.art: A long paper strip dipped in one katori with a dark end fading to a pale end.
setup.caption: 2. Another idea: dip one end and let the dye fade along the strip.

setup.art: A finished strip with three bands, dark, medium and pale, taped together, and a friend pointing to the medium band.
setup.caption: 3. Test your strip. Can someone name the bands?
