flow.do: Read the problem together. Look back at the strips from the Colour Map test. Ask how to get three clear bands from one dye.
flow.say: You have one dye and no brush. Make a strip with three clear bands. What could you change to get a dark band, a medium band and a pale band?
flow.kid: Make a strip with three clear bands from one dye. What could you change?

ask.q: What could you change to make the dye lighter or darker?

flow.context: This is the first step of Three Stripes From One Dye. You think about the problem.

flow.do: Test two ideas on short strips. Write down what you did and what you got.
flow.say: Choose two ideas and test them on small strips. Write down what you did and how each strip looked.
flow.kid: Test two ideas. Write what you did. Look at the bands.
flow.parent: The method with three katoris and 12, 6 and 3 drops is called a dilution series. Scientists use it often. It almost always gives clear bands. A single dipped strip may give a smooth fade, and not three clear bands.
flow.context: In this step, you test two ideas for making three bands.

flow.do: Pick the best strip. Ask someone who has not seen it to say which band is dark, which is medium and which is pale. Talk about why it worked.
flow.say: Show your best strip to someone who has not seen it. Ask them to point to the dark, the medium and the pale band. Did it work?
flow.kid: Show your best strip to someone. Can they find the dark, medium and pale bands?
flow.parent: Cells can switch on a gene only when the signal is above a certain amount. That turns a smooth change into clear steps. After they have shared their idea, say so.
flow.think: A real embryo makes sharp bands from a smooth signal. How might cells turn a smooth fade into clear bands?
flow.context: This is the last step of Three Stripes From One Dye. You test your strip with someone new.

items.p: Which statement about the cells in your body is true?
opts: Nearly all of them hold the same DNA, but each kind uses different genes
Each kind of cell holds different DNA
Only brain cells hold DNA
items.why: You began as one cell, and every copy of the DNA was passed on to the new cells. A skin cell and a nerve cell hold the same genes but switch on different ones. Picking 'different DNA' means thinking that the cells lost genes as they changed.

items.p: A skin cell and a nerve cell in the same person hold different genes.
items.why: False. They hold the same genes. The difference is that cells of each kind use only the genes for their own job.

items.p: A signal that gets ____ as you move away from its source can help cells find where they are.
items.why: A signal spreads out from its source, so cells close by receive more and cells far away receive less. The amount tells a cell how far away the source is.

items.p: Match each word to its meaning.
pairs: a cell that can make new cells and has not settled on a final job
the organ that passes oxygen and food between the mother's blood and the baby's blood
cells dying on purpose when a signal tells them to
items.why: These four words describe four parts of growing: instructions, cells that can still change, the meeting place for two bloodstreams, and the cells that leave on purpose.

items.p: In a model of a growing embryo, a row of paper pieces gets dye from one end. What decides how dark each piece is?
opts: How far the piece is from the dye
What the piece is called
What is written on the piece
items.why: The dye fades with distance, so the closer pieces are darker. A real embryo works in the same way: the amount of signal that reaches a cell depends on how far away the source is.

items.p: Sort each event by whether it happens before birth or after birth.
items: the placenta passes oxygen to the baby
items.why: The heart and hands are built in the first eight weeks, and the placenta feeds the baby until birth. Breathing air, the belly button and smiling come after birth.

items.p: A healthy baby is 50 centimetres long at birth and 75 centimetres long at one year. By how many centimetres did the baby grow?
items.why: 75 take away 50 is 25. In the first year, a baby grows about half as much again as their length at birth.

items.p: Explain in your own words how cells in an embryo can find out where they are, using a signal that fades with distance.
items.a: A signal comes from a small group of cells and spreads out. Cells near the source get a lot of it. Cells farther away get less. Each cell can sense how much has reached them, and that tells them how far away they are, and so what job to take.
items.why: A strong answer says that the signal gets weaker with distance, and that a cell can sense the amount. It may also say that the amount decides the cell's job.

items.p: Which is the odd one out, and why? The gaps between fingers, a tadpole's tail going, a cut on your knee healing, the gaps between a chick's toes.
items.a: A cut healing, because new cells grow to fill the gap. In the other three, cells die on purpose to leave a gap.
items.why: Fingers, a tadpole's tail and a chick's toes all involve cells that die on a signal. Healing is cells being made.

items.p: Why can a baby's blood take oxygen from the mother's blood in the placenta?
opts: The baby's haemoglobin holds oxygen more tightly than the mother's does
The two bloods mix together
The mother's blood is pumped into the baby's body
items.why: The two bloods run close together but do not mix. The baby's blood holds oxygen more tightly, so oxygen passes across the thin wall. Picking 'mix' misses the thin wall that keeps the two bloodstreams apart.

items.p: Draw three stages of a hand forming: a flat paddle, a paddle with finger lines, and five separate fingers. Mark the cells that die.
items.a: Three small drawings in order: a flat paddle shape, a paddle with faint lines, five fingers. The gaps between the lines are marked or shaded.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the gaps between the finger lines as the place where cells die, and not as places where something is cut.

items.p: Put these steps in order, for how a baby gets oxygen before birth.
a: Oxygen goes from her lungs into her blood
Oxygen crosses the thin wall in the placenta
The baby's blood carries it along the cord to the baby
items.why: Oxygen travels in a chain. The wall in the placenta is where it moves from the mother's blood to the baby's blood. The cord then carries the baby's blood back to the baby.

items.p: The mother's blood flows straight through the cord into the baby's body.
items.why: False. The two bloods run close together in the placenta, but they do not mix. Oxygen and food cross a thin wall, and the cord carries the baby's own blood.

items.p: You practise writing with your other hand every day for a week. What is happening in your brain?
opts: The connections you use get stronger
Your brain grows a new part
Your nerve cells are replaced by new ones
items.why: Each time you write, the connections between the nerve cells you use get stronger, so the movement gets faster. A brain does not grow a new part for a new skill.

items.p: A friend says: 'My nose is just like my father's, so my genes decided everything about me.'

views.says: My nose looks just like my father's, and my sister's looks like my mother's. Genes decide who we are.
Genes matter a lot for the shape of a nose. But height, health and skills also depend on food, care and practice.
My students have different genes, and they learn different things, because of what they do each day.

items.ask: Whose view do you agree with most? What evidence would help you decide?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer picks a view and gives a reason. It may mention that identical twins have the same genes but are not the same, or that well-fed children grow taller.
items.why: This question has no single right answer. Genes and surroundings both shape a person, and scientists still argue about how much each counts. What matters is your reason.

items.p: A baby grows fastest in the womb and in the first ____ years of life.
items.why: A baby grows about 25 centimetres in the first year and about 12 in the second. After that, growth slows to about five or six centimetres a year.

items.p: A young child's brain has more connections between nerve cells than an adult's brain.
items.why: True. A young child's brain makes far more connections than it keeps. Those used often are made stronger, and those not used are removed.

items.p: A scientist moves a small piece of an early embryo to the belly of another embryo, and a second body starts to form there. What does this show?
opts: The piece sends signals that tell the neighbouring cells what to become
The piece turns into the whole second body by itself
Every embryo can grow two bodies
items.why: In Hilde Mangold's experiment, most of the second body was made from the host's own cells. The piece did not become the body. It told its neighbours what to become.

items.p: A cell from a tadpole's gut is put into an egg cell, and a whole frog grows. What does this show about the gut cell?
opts: It still holds every instruction for building a frog
It was already part of a frog's egg
Gut cells are the same as egg cells
items.why: The frog could only grow if the cell held all the instructions. So the gut cell had kept every gene, even though the cell used only a few.

items.p: A model has to be exactly like the real thing to be useful.
items.why: False. A model is useful when it shows one idea clearly. The dye strip shows how a fading signal can set jobs, though real cells use chemicals and have many more jobs.

items.p: A change that goes smoothly from a lot to a little over a distance is called a ____.
items.why: A gradient is a smooth change over a distance. The amount of a signal falling away from its source is a gradient.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
pairs: a soft spot in a baby's skull
a firm but bendy material that is softer than bone
the layer where a long bone grows longer
the red protein that holds oxygen in red blood cells
items.why: These are four parts of a growing body. The soft spots let the head squeeze through birth, cartilage hardens into bone, growth plates lengthen the bones, and haemoglobin carries the oxygen.

items.p: Sort each event by whether it needs cells to die or cells to multiply.
items: the gaps between the fingers form
the gaps between a chick's toes form
a graze on your arm heals
a growing child's skin gets bigger
items.why: A body is built both by making cells and by removing them. Fingers, toes and a tadpole's tail are shaped by cell death. Growing bones, healing skin and a growing body need more cells.

items.p: A baby gains 6 centimetres between 3 and 6 months, and 4 centimetres between 6 and 9 months. How many more centimetres did the baby gain in the first of these two periods?
items.why: 6 take away 4 is 2. The baby gained 2 centimetres more in the earlier period, which shows that growth is slowing.

items.p: A friend says: 'Practising is pointless. Either you have it or you don't.' What would you say, using what you know about the brain?
items.a: Practice makes the connections between nerve cells that you use stronger, so the skill gets faster and easier. A young brain has many connections, and the ones you use are kept. Even skills that feel hard at first get easier with practice.
items.why: A strong answer says that practice strengthens the connections that are used. It may add that unused connections fade.

items.p: Which one is not a model? A clay placenta, a paper strip with fading dye, a real placenta, a computer drawing of a heart.
items.a: A real placenta, because it is the real thing. The other three stand in for something else to show an idea.
items.why: A model is a stand-in. A real placenta is the actual organ.

items.p: Draw a row of six cells with a signal source at the left end. Shade each cell to show how much signal reaches that cell, and label three different jobs.
items.a: Six cells in a row, the leftmost darkest and the rightmost palest, with three labels such as 'job A' near the source, 'job B' in the middle and 'job C' far from it.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the shading getting steadily paler away from the source, and the jobs changing in steps along the row.

items.p: Put these steps in order, for how a skill becomes easier with practice.
a: You try the skill for the first time
Signals pass along a path of nerve cells
Each time you repeat it, the connections along that path get stronger
The path works faster and with less effort
Connections you do not use fade away
items.why: Practice strengthens the connections you use. This takes many repeats. Unused connections fade after that.

items.p: At birth the baby's lungs are filled with fluid. What happens at the first breath?
opts: Air opens the lungs and blood starts to flow through them
The lungs fill with milk
The cord starts to carry air
items.why: Before birth the lungs hold fluid and the placenta supplies oxygen. At the first breath, air opens the lungs and blood flows through them. The small shortcuts in the heart then close.

items.p: A friend says: 'Cells dying in a body must mean something has gone wrong.'

views.says: If cells die, the body must be damaged or ill. Dying is bad.
Cells also die on purpose. That is how fingers and toes get separated. Without it, hands would stay as paddles.
I prune my plants so they grow better. Taking away a part can help the whole.

items.ask: Whose view fits the evidence best? What would you tell the friend?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer picks the scientist's view, and may mention fingers, or a tadpole's tail, as evidence that cell death can be a normal part of building.
items.why: There are two kinds of cell death. Some cells die from damage. Others die on a signal, as part of building a body. Both are real, and the second is normal and needed.

items.p: A growth graph of a baby's length is steep at the start and flat later on. What does this show?
opts: The baby grows fastest when very young, and then more slowly
The baby stops growing at six months
The baby is growing the same amount each month
items.why: A steep line means fast growth, and a flatter line means slower growth. A baby grows fastest in the first months and slows down. The line does not go flat, because growing carries on.

items.p: Identical twins have the same genes and exactly the same fingerprints.
items.why: False. Identical twins have the same genes, but their fingerprints are different. The surroundings in the womb and small chances shape the details.

items.p: The scar left by the cord after birth is called the ____.
items.why: The cord carried blood between the baby and the placenta. After birth it is no longer needed, and the small scar it leaves is the belly button.

items.p: Early in development, a patch of cells that was going to become skin is moved to the part that becomes the brain. What is it likely to become?
opts: Brain tissue, because early cells follow their new neighbours
Skin, because it was already fixed
Nothing, because it would die
items.why: Early cells have not settled on their jobs, so they follow the signals of their new neighbours. Later cells keep their old job even when moved.

items.p: A friend says: 'Piece 1 of a paper strip is dark because it is a dark piece. It was born dark.' How could you test whether the position, and not the piece, decides the colour?
items.a: Cut two strips from the same paper. Dip one at the left end and one at the right end. If piece 1 is dark on one strip and pale on the other, it is the position that matters.
items.why: A strong answer changes only the end that gets the dye, uses the same paper, and compares the same piece on the two strips. Then the piece itself cannot be the cause.

items.p: A baby grows from 50 centimetres at birth to 75 centimetres at one year, and to 87 centimetres at two years. How many more centimetres did the baby grow in the first year than in the second?
items.why: The first year gained 25 centimetres. The second year gained 12. 25 take away 12 is 13. The baby grew 13 centimetres more in the first year.

items.p: Dye goes into a paper strip at both ends at the same time. Where on the strip is the colour palest?
opts: In the middle
At both ends
Next to the left end
items.why: The dye fades with distance from each end. The middle is the farthest point from both sources, so it is the palest. Real bodies use the same trick to make symmetrical parts.

items.p: Two identical twins have the same genes. One is 4 centimetres taller than the other at age ten. Why?

views.says: One twin may have eaten better, or been healthier as a baby. Food and health change how tall a body grows.
Small chances in the womb, such as how much food each twin got, can leave lasting differences, even with the same genes.
Both of my children are growing well. A few centimetres of difference between twins is not unusual.

items.ask: Whose reason seems most likely to you? What would you want to find out?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer picks a reason, and says what to check, such as the birth weights, the food, or illnesses.
items.why: Genes give the same plan to both twins, but food, health and chance change how the plan is used. Scientists still study how much each counts.

items.p: A skin cell and a heart muscle cell are looked at closely. What would you expect to find about their DNA?
opts: The same genes in both
Different genes in each
DNA only in the heart cell
items.why: Both cells came from the same first cell, and they hold the same set of genes. They differ in which genes they use.

items.p: A baby can have a different blood group from their mother.
items.why: True. The two bloodstreams run close together but do not mix. If they simply mixed, a baby's blood group would have to be the same as the mother's.

items.p: A model shows an idea clearly, but it is not exactly the ____ thing.
items.why: A model leaves out many details, so it can show one idea. It is a stand-in for the real thing, which is always more complicated.

items.p: Match each situation to the idea it shows.
pairs: A frog grows from a gut cell's DNA
every cell holds all the instructions
A paper strip is dark near the dye and pale far from it
A child writes faster after each try
items.why: Each situation is a small piece of evidence for one idea in this unit.

items.p: Sort each fact by whether it is true of a newborn, an adult, or both.
items: the same DNA in nearly every cell
cartilage in the nose and ear
a wrist made mostly of cartilage
items.why: A newborn has more, softer pieces, and some join and harden as the child grows. Nearly every cell holds the same DNA at any age, and the nose and ear keep their cartilage for life.

items.p: A friend says: 'The paper strip proves exactly how cells in an embryo work.' What is the best reply?
opts: It is a model. It shows a fading signal, but real cells use chemicals and have many more jobs
You are right. Real cells work exactly like paper
Models cannot teach us anything
items.why: A model can show an idea without being exactly like the real thing. Scientists use models, and then check them against real embryos.

items.p: Which one does not get weaker as you move away from its source? The smell of tadka, the warmth of a lamp, the length of a ruler, the sound of a drum.
items.a: The length of a ruler. It stays the same wherever you stand.
items.why: Smell, warmth and sound all spread out and fade with distance. A ruler's length is not a signal at all.

items.p: Explain why a body needs some cells to die, using fingers as your example.
items.a: A hand starts as a flat paddle. Without the cells between the finger lines dying, the fingers would stay joined. Cells dying on a signal leaves five separate fingers.
items.why: A strong answer says that the cells between the finger lines die on a signal, and that this makes the fingers separate. It may say that building a body is both adding and taking away.

items.p: Draw the placenta as a model: two bloodstreams close together with a thin wall between them. Use arrows to show oxygen and waste.
items.a: Two channels side by side, one labelled mother's blood and one labelled baby's blood, with a thin line between. An arrow for oxygen goes from the mother's side to the baby's. An arrow for waste goes the other way.
items.why: A strong drawing keeps the two bloodstreams apart, with a wall between them, and shows oxygen going to the baby and carbon dioxide going back.

items.p: Put these steps in order, for how a flat paddle becomes five fingers.
a: The hand is a flat paddle
A signal reaches the cells between the finger lines
The cells between the finger lines die
items.why: The cells must get the signal before they die, and the fingers can only separate after the gaps open.

items.p: Why might learning a new language be easier at age three than at age thirty?
opts: A young brain has many more connections, and keeps the ones that are used
Young children are cleverer than adults
Adults have no connections left
items.why: A young brain has far more connections than it will keep. The ones used often get stronger, and the others fade. Picking 'cleverer' is a common mistake. It is about the number of connections, and not about being smarter.

items.p: A well-fed child in Norway and a well-fed child in India grow in very similar ways.
items.why: True. The World Health Organization measured healthy, well-fed children in six countries and found that they grew in almost the same way. Food, health and care matter much more than where a child lives.

items.p: One cell splits in two. Each of those splits in two, and so on. After 5 rounds of splitting, how many cells are there?
items.why: The numbers go 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32. Each round doubles the number of cells.

quiz.p: A skin cell and a nerve cell look and work differently, though they hold the same DNA. Why?
opts: Each kind of cell uses a different set of the genes
They hold different DNA
Nerve cells have no DNA
quiz.why: Both cells came from one first cell and kept all the genes. A skin cell uses the genes for skin, and a nerve cell uses the genes for nerves.

quiz.p: In an early embryo, what mostly tells a cell which job to take?
opts: Signals from nearby cells, and how strong they are at that spot
A label stuck on the cell at birth
The size of the cell
quiz.why: Signals spread out from some cells and fade with distance. A cell reads how much has reached them, and that gives them a job that fits their place.

quiz.p: A scientist changes the dye strength and also the paper in the same test. What is the problem?
opts: She cannot tell which change caused the result
The test will take longer
There is no problem
quiz.why: A fair test changes one thing at a time. If two things change, any difference could come from either.

quiz.p: How does oxygen get from the mother to the baby before birth?
opts: It crosses a thin wall in the placenta from the mother's blood to the baby's blood
The baby breathes it in from the water
It travels through the baby's mouth
quiz.why: The baby's lungs are full of fluid before birth. Oxygen crosses the thin wall in the placenta, and the cord carries the baby's blood back to the baby.

quiz.p: What happens to a baby's blood at the first breath?
opts: It begins to flow through the lungs
It stops flowing
It mixes with the mother's blood
quiz.why: Before birth most blood skips the lungs. At the first breath the lungs open and blood starts to pour through them. The shortcuts in the heart close within days.

quiz.p: Which of these is made by cells dying on purpose?
opts: The gaps between the fingers
The nails on the fingers
The bones of the fingers
quiz.why: A hand begins as a flat paddle. Cells between the finger lines die on a signal, and that leaves separate fingers. Nails and bones are made by growing cells.

quiz.p: A line graph of a baby's length is steepest where?
opts: In the first months after birth
At two years old
It has the same slope everywhere
quiz.why: A baby gains about 11 centimetres in the first three months and about 4 centimetres in the three months after the ninth month. The line is steepest early and flatter later.

quiz.p: A child's growth line is below another child's, but they follow their own line steadily. What does this mean?
opts: They are probably growing well
They are growing badly
They have stopped growing
quiz.why: Healthy children follow their own lines, and the lines are often different. What matters is a steady path, and not how close it is to someone else's.

quiz.p: Which helps a skill become easier?
opts: Repeating it, so the connections you use get stronger
Waiting for a new brain part to grow
Doing it once, very hard
quiz.why: Repeating a skill strengthens the connections you use. This is why practice works. The line of improvement flattens as the easy gains are used up.

quiz.p: Why might a scientist mark the cells of a moved piece with a different colour from the host?
opts: To tell which cells came from the piece and which belonged to the host
To make the picture prettier
To stop the cells dividing
quiz.why: Marking lets the scientist see what the moved piece became and what the neighbours built. That shows whether the piece made the new body, or told its neighbours to build it.

opts: One ball of cells that splits in two
Two separate egg cells
One baby that is cut in half
quiz.why: Early cells are not yet fixed on their jobs, so each half can build a whole baby. Non-identical twins begin as two separate egg cells.

quiz.p: A row of cells gets a signal from one end. Which cell gets the most signal?
opts: The one closest to the source
The one farthest from the source
They all get the same
quiz.why: A signal fades with distance. The closest cell gets the most, and the farthest cell gets the least.

applications: Doctors use growth charts to see whether a baby or child is growing steadily along their own line.
Ultrasound scans let doctors watch a baby's heart and body parts form before birth.
Doctors treat babies born with joined fingers, because they understand how fingers form.
Stem cell treatments, such as bone marrow transplants, replace blood cells in people with some illnesses.
Advice to pregnant women about food, medicines and alcohol is based on what can cross the placenta.
Doctors use the X-ray of a wrist to estimate how old a child's bones are.
Teachers use practice in short, regular bursts, because brains strengthen the connections they use.
Developmental biologists study how signals set cell jobs, to learn how to prevent birth defects.
Scientists grow small clumps of cells in a dish, called organoids, to study how organs form.
Hospitals keep premature babies warm and give them extra oxygen while their lungs finish growing.

open_questions.q: How does a growing body know when to stop, so that each organ ends up the right size?
open_questions.why_open: Cells divide in response to signals, but scientists do not yet understand how the whole organ knows its final size.

open_questions.q: How do cells decide to take a job, and not just follow a signal? What is the role of chance?
open_questions.why_open: Signals set the main pattern, but individual cells also show random differences. Scientists are still working out how much chance matters.

open_questions.q: Why do human babies grow so fast in the womb and the first two years, and then slow down?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have several ideas, such as the cost of energy and the risks of birth. They have not agreed on a single reason.

open_questions.q: How does the early experience of a baby leave marks on the body that last for life?
open_questions.why_open: The Dutch Hunger Winter showed that early hunger affects health later. How the marks are stored is still being studied.

open_questions.q: Could we one day grow new organs from a person's own stem cells?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have grown small clumps of organ-like tissue. Growing a whole working organ is much harder, and nobody knows if it will work.

open_questions.q: Why do some cells keep their ability to become many kinds, while most settle for life?
open_questions.why_open: We know many of the switches involved, but we do not yet know the full story of why most cells never go back.

maths.problem: A baby's length is 50 cm at birth, 61 cm at 3 months and 67 cm at 6 months. How many more centimetres did the baby gain in the first three months than in the next three months?
maths.explain: In the first three months the baby gained 61 minus 50, which is 11 cm. In the next three months the baby gained 67 minus 61, which is 6 cm. 11 minus 6 is 5. The baby gained 5 cm more in the first three months.
maths.context: In the My Growth Line activity, you draw a graph of a baby's length from birth to two years.
maths.why_maths: Finding the gain in each step shows you where the line is steepest, and so when growth is fastest.

maths.problem: A ball of cells doubles in number each round: 1, 2, 4, 8, and so on. How many cells are there after 10 rounds? Then, since 10 rounds multiply the number by about 1,000, say roughly how many rounds make a million million.
maths.answer: 1,024 cells after 10 rounds. About 40 rounds make a million million.
maths.explain: The numbers go 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512, and then 1,024 after 10 rounds. So every 10 rounds multiplies the number by about 1,000. Four lots of 10 rounds make 1,000 times 1,000 times 1,000 times 1,000, which is a million million. A body of about 30 trillion cells needs around 45 rounds of doubling, in a rough sum. In real bodies, not all cells divide, and many die.
maths.context: A human body began as one cell, and now has about 30 trillion cells.
maths.why_maths: Doubling grows far faster than it first seems, and this is how a single cell can become trillions in a few dozen rounds.

maths.problem: A paper strip is cut into 6 equal pieces. The 2 pieces next to the dye are dark, the next 2 are medium, and the last 2 are pale. What fraction of the strip is pale? Write it in its simplest form.
maths.explain: 2 out of 6 pieces are pale. That is 2 over 6. Divide the top and the bottom by 2, to get 1 over 3.
maths.context: In the Colour Map test, you cut a strip into pieces and give each piece a job.
maths.why_maths: Fractions let you say how much of the strip each job takes up, and compare strips of different lengths.

maths.problem: A newborn's brain weighs about 350 grams. An adult's brain weighs about 1,400 grams. How many times heavier is an adult's brain?
maths.explain: 1,400 divided by 350 is 4. So the newborn's brain is about a quarter of the weight of an adult's. By age five, it is about nine-tenths of the adult weight.
maths.context: A child's brain grows quickly before the age of five, while the body keeps growing for years.
maths.why_maths: Dividing one weight by another shows how many times bigger one is, and helps you see how fast the brain grows compared with the body.

maths.problem: The heart starts to beat in week 3 of growing, and the baby is born in week 38. For how many weeks does the heart beat before birth? How many days is that?
maths.explain: 38 minus 3 is 35 weeks. There are 7 days in a week, and 35 times 7 is 245. The heart beats for about 245 days before the baby is born.
maths.context: In growing, the heart is one of the first parts to begin working.
maths.why_maths: Changing weeks into days lets you compare the time a body part has been working with the days in a calendar.

maths.problem: Your bone marrow makes about 2 million new red blood cells every second. How many is that in one minute? How many in ten minutes?
maths.answer: 120 million in a minute, and 1,200 million in ten minutes.
maths.explain: There are 60 seconds in a minute. 2 million times 60 is 120 million. For ten minutes, 120 million times 10 is 1,200 million, which is also called 1.2 billion.
maths.context: A body keeps making new cells all through life, to replace the ones that wear out.
maths.why_maths: Very large numbers become easier when you build them step by step from a number you can imagine, such as two million.

maths.problem: Divya, a girl in Class 4 in Kochi, times herself writing a line with her left hand. Her times are 38, 31, 27, 25, 24 and 24 seconds. How many seconds did she save between the first and the sixth try? Which try saved the most time?
maths.answer: 14 seconds. The second try saved the most, with 7 seconds.
maths.explain: 38 minus 24 is 14 seconds. From try 1 to try 2 she saved 38 minus 31, which is 7 seconds. The later tries saved 4, 2, 1 and 0 seconds. The savings get smaller each time.
maths.context: In the Wrong-Hand test, you time yourself writing a line six times and draw a line graph.
maths.why_maths: Finding how much was saved on each try shows the shape of the graph: big gains first and smaller gains later.

maths.problem: In one often-quoted estimate, a placenta has a folded surface of about 12 square metres. A room is 4 metres long and 3 metres wide. What is the area of the room? Is it more or less than the placenta's surface?
maths.answer: 12 square metres. It is about the same.
maths.explain: The area of a room is length times width. 4 times 3 is 12 square metres. The folded surface of the placenta has about the same area as the floor of this room, though it fits into a flat organ the size of a dinner plate.
maths.context: The placenta's thin, folded fingers give it a very large surface for passing oxygen and food.
maths.why_maths: Area tells you how much surface there is for oxygen and food to cross, and why folding a surface packs a lot of it into a small space.

how_we_found_out.story: In 1888 the German scientist Wilhelm Roux killed one of the two cells of a frog egg with a hot needle. The other cell grew into half an embryo, so he said every cell is fixed from the start. In 1891 Hans Driesch separated sea urchin cells, and each grew into a whole small animal. So who was right? In Freiburg, Hilde Mangold, a young student of Hans Spemann, tried a new test. She chose a pale newt and a dark newt, so she could tell their cells apart. She took a small piece from the back of the pale embryo and placed it on the belly of the dark one. The dark host grew a second body, a twin joined to the first. Most of the new body was made of the host's own cells. The piece had not become the second body. It had told its neighbours what to become. The paper came out in 1924. That same year Hilde Mangold, still in her twenties, died after a fire accident at home. Spemann won the Nobel Prize in 1935 for the discovery. The name 'organiser' came from this work.
how_we_found_out.who: Hilde Mangold and Hans Spemann, building on Wilhelm Roux and Hans Driesch
how_we_found_out.when: 1888 (Roux), 1891 (Driesch) and 1924 (the year Mangold and Spemann's paper came out)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Roux said cells are fixed on their jobs from the start, because half an embryo grew from one live cell. Driesch showed that cells from an early embryo can each make a whole animal. Mangold showed that a small group of cells tells their neighbours what to become.

playtest: I could not run the experiments here, so this is a desk check, step by step, with a flat's kitchen in mind. Colour Map (e1): paper towel, food colour, two katoris and a tray are all common. The result depends on the dye strength and the paper. The steps say to use the dye front as the clock, to lift the strip at piece 5, and what to do if the strip comes out all dark (add water and use a new strip) or all pale (add drops). I have not seen the fade on a real strip, so a parent should try one strip first. Wrong-Hand Writing (e2): needs only a pen, paper and a clock. Most people speed up in the first three tries, and the steps say what to do if a time goes up. Hand activity: raw dough should not be eaten, and the knife is blunt. Timeline Detective: all 22 cards are written out, with typical ages and a note that babies differ. Played with 1 to 4 players in my head: alone, count points out of 21. The family interviews are optional for families without elders nearby, and ask only what people want to share. Three Stripes: the three-katori dilution method should always work, and the single-dip method may only give a smooth fade. Facts to check before this goes out: the placenta's villous surface of about 12 square metres (varies by source), the typical lengths used in My Growth Line (rounded from WHO medians, average of boys and girls), the 'week' numbers on the timeline cards (counted from when the baby began, not from the mother's last period), Mangold's age and the details of her death, the claim that the duck's webbing comes from fewer cells dying, and the newborn brain weight of about 350 grams. No video was checked, because no ids are filled in.
